entries.english: Archaic Kingozi / Kiamu Poetic Vocabulary from "Hadithi ya Liongo", "Mashairi ya Liongo" (by Sheikh Abdallah Muyuweni), "Utumbuizo wa Gungu" & "Mwanzo wa Utenzi wa Ayubu" (Steere 1870 pp. 439–488)
entries.translation: Hadithi ya Liongo (pp. 439–453, prose narrative told by Hamisi wa Kayi of Liongo Fumo of Shanga and Ozi on the Kenyan coast, his 6-line prison song to his slave-girl "Ewe kijakazi nakutuma uwatumika... Afanye mkate, pale kati tupa kaweka, Nikeze pingu na minyoo ikinyoka", p. 442; the kikoa cha makoma palm-fruit trap and couplet "Kukuingia hadaani Liongo fumo si mtu, Yunga jini Liongo okoka", p. 448; his betrayal with a copper needle in the navel sindano ya shaba ya kitovu after singing "Mimi muyi ndimi mwe mao, sitae", p. 450; and his death kneeling with drawn bow at the wells of Ozi, where his grave is still seen, p. 452) • Mashairi ya Liongo (pp. 455–471, 5-line takhmisi stanzas composed by Sheikh Abdallah bin Ali bin Nasir Muyuweni of the house of Sheikh Ali bin Abubakr bin Salim, presented in archaic Kingozi/Kiamu alongside common Swahili: "Tufutufu mayi kizimbwini yawanguruma; ha'mwezi kwima luishapo wimbi Ungama", p. 462; "Si simba mikia wameao vuzi na singa; simba mashujaa wasahili ngozi na nyama", p. 468) • Utumbuizo wa Gungu (pp. 473–483, two ancient wedding dance songs in Kingozi & common Swahili: (1) Gungu la Kufunda "Pounding Figure" praising the bride Mananazi, serving Indian pilao ya zabibu on a Persian tray sinia ya Shirazi with water-cooler guduwia, and chewing betel leaf tambuu ya Siu and soft betel of Ozi layini ya Ozi with cardamom iliki and almonds lozi, pp. 474–481; (2) Gungu la Kukwaa "Stumbling Figure" praising the ornaments of Ungama, gold frontlets sarufo, bracelets vitindi/timbi, collars kama/vidani, and warning against the Comoro man Mugazidja na kubu/kopo and the Galla warrior with his bow "Kujile Mgala na mata na mata, Ujile kutaka kuteta / Tutawekilia ukuta, Wasituingilie myini", pp. 480–483) • Mwanzo wa Utenzi wa Ayubu (pp. 485–487, 5-stanza prologue to the Epic of Job: "Akhi pani karatasi / Na wino mema mweusi / Na kalamu ya unyasi... Kwa Kiswahili choma")
entries.context: Bishop Edward Steere (1870) 'Swahili Tales, as Told by Natives of Zanzibar', pp. 439–488

entries.translation: Siku ya muaka / Nerus / Neroz (around August 24th, p. 338: bathing in the sea at dawn, communal feast, and dancing ngóma ya shíndoa around a fire beating the ground with bamboos chanting: 'tújile ku tía motto Teita na múme tulimpeta Hamade', p. 332) • Muóngo (pl. mióngo, p. 268: 10-day agricultural decades reckoned from Siku ya muaka, 3 mióngo per month through muongo sabaini and up to 360 days) • 3 Harvests: Muaka (August harvest of mtama, mahindi, mpunga, kunde, pojo sown in masika, p. 258), Mjō (Oct–Nov harvest of crops sown in fúli, p. 230), and Fuli (latter rains July–Aug, p. 73) • 6 Seasons (m'simu, p. 248): Musimi/kazkazi (Dec–Feb NE monsoon), Masíka (March–May heavy rains), Kipúpue (May–June cold season), Damani/muaka (Aug harvest), Kussi (SW monsoon), Tanga mbili / Malelezi (March–May & Oct–Nov variable winds when vessels sail both N and S, pp. 196, 358)

entries.english: Dr. L. Krapf's (1882, pp. xiii–xl) Outline of a Suahili Grammar: 8 Noun Classes, Post-Prefixes (Genitive), 6 Verb Derivatives & Classical Kimvita Salutations
entries.translation: 8 Noun Classes in 3 Divisions (pp. xiv–xvii): (A) Prefixed: Class I m-/wa- (mtu/watu), Class II m-/mi- (mti/miti); (B) In Part-prefixed: Class III -/Ø (niumba), Class IV -/ma- (neno/maneno), Class V ch-, ki-/vi- (kitu/vitu), Class VI u-/Ø, ni-, ma-, mb-, nd- (ulimi/ndimi, ufunguo/funguo, ubao/mbao); (C) Non-prefixed: Class VII máhali/muáhali (pa/mua/kua), Class VIII ku- (kuffa kuangu) • Post-prefixes (p. xxi): Krapf coins 'post-prefix' for the genitive particle (wa, ya, la, cha, via, za, pa, mua, kua, derived from ku-a 'to be') • 6 Verb Derivatives (pp. xxiii–xxiv): Simple (ku penda), Causative (-sa/-za/-sha: ku pendéza), Objective/Dative (-ia/-ea: ku pendéa), Reflexive (ji-: ku-ji-penda), Reciprocal (-na: ku pendána), Iterative (-le-/-li-: ku pendeléa), plus Kimvita passive -oa (ku pendoa), 1st sg. future tapenda, object suffixes (-mi, -we, -e, -sui, -nui, -o), and ambai kuamba relatives • Classical Salutations by Time & Rank (pp. xx–xxi): Daybreak 'kuna kuja / kume kaja' → Morning 'Ujeléwe? — Náwe ujeléwe? / Tumejeléwa' → Noon 'Za mtana? — Ni héri, uamba záko' → General 'Uháli gani? — Haliyangu ngema, kama lulu, kama marjáni, kama fethaluka' → Evening 'Kuna kútua — Ku lituelle, ninende nikalále, kua heri ya Muigni zimgu' (also ku tuésha evening visit, p. 381) → Subordinate 'Nashika móu Bana/Muigni/Muána/Muunguána — ai / marhaba — nimekwisho shikamóu'

entries.translation: 12 Swahili Lunar Months (mfungúo, p. 224): (1) Mfungúo wa mosi (Shawwal), (2) Mfungúo wa pili (Dhu al-Qa'dah), (3) Mfungúo wa tatu (Dhu al-Hijjah), (4) Mfungúo wa nne (Muharram), (5) Mfungúo wa tano (Safar), (6) Mfungúo wa sitta (Rabi' I), (7) Mfungúo wa sabaa (Rabi' II), (8) Mfungúo wa nane (Jumada I), (9) Mfungúo wa kenda (Jumada II), (10) Régeb (Rajab, p. 314), (11) Shabāan / muezi wa mlísho (month of feeding, pp. 224, 327), (12) Ramathani / muezi wa t'ummu / saúmu (fasting month, pp. 224, 324, 385) • 5 Growth Stages of the Coconut after Blossom (punga, p. 311; dáfu, p. 43; kidáka, p. 138; nasi, p. 273; púnje, p. 313): (1) kidáka (pl. vidáka, tiny embryo nut), (2) kitále (pl. vitále, half-ripe shell forming), (3) dafu (pl. madafu, full of sweet water; sub-stages punje/búpu la dafu = urambirambi soft jelly vs. tonga la dafu with firm flesh), (4) kórŏma (pl. makóroma, water decreasing, kernel hardening), (5) nazi (ripe nut; mbáta dried copra, kisímŭi sprouted nut, joya spongy kernel, tui la kassiméle first-pressed cream vs. taki/jija strained residue, pp. 355, 381) • 5 Names of the Fingers (chanda p. 34, jánda p. 112): (1) chanda cha gumba (thumb), (2) chanda cha sháhada / sháhuda (forefinger/index), (3) chanda cha tokā (middle finger, used to apply lime in uraibu), (4) chanda cha kati ya kando / cha muandamízi wa misho (ring finger), (5) chanda cha misho / cha kando (little finger) • 3 Personal Names in a Swahili Life (jína p. 117, sáre p. 324): (1) jina la ufiazi / la ku vialíwa nálo / jina la sare (birth-name, often by day of birth: Muegni Matáno [Wed], Muegni Hamisi [Thu], Mosse [Sat], Muapili [Sun], Muatatu [Mon], Muegniámmé [Tue], Muegni jumáa [Fri]), (2) jina la ku tahiriwa (circumcision-name given at kumbi/tohara), (3) jina la mke / la maózi (marriage-name assumed at wedding)

entries.english: Multilingual Names of Mombasa (Mvita) & the Jub River, Legend of Shehe Mvita, the 3 Petrified Sabbath-Breakers & Submerged Ungama (Krapf 1882)
entries.translation: Multilingual Names of Mombasa (kongowéa p. 170, mombas p. 240, mvita p. 270): Swahili Mvita / Mwita, Kongowéa, Fáladi, Mombasa; Wanika Kiziwáni; Kamba Kidiamóni; Sambara Ngoméni; Galla Worra Mombása (alongside Galla Worra Wárdisa [Ozi], Worra Lanne [Lamu], Worra Hawinne [Patta]); Galla ethnonyms (múnio p. 267, wátoa p. 425): Múnio (Pokomo on the Dana), Dunga (Europeans/Banians), Mulusho (Arabs), Hamára (Swahili); Kamba call the Galla Wátoa (from Galla wato 'sorcerers/diviners'); Waata/Dahalo names (wasánie p. 424, sosobráni p. 345): Kigunia Wadahálo, Kimvita Wasánie, Kinika Ariangúlo • 4 Names of the Jub River (jūb p. 121, vumbo p. 420): Arabic Jūb, Swahili Wúmbu / Vumbo (upper course Godshob), Galla Danisa, Somali Gowinda • Legend of Shehe Mvita (mvita, p. 270): First autochthonous settler of Mombasa ('Shehe Mvita alisuka katika nti, alitimbúka katika Mvita') who built the northern town opposite Kizaúni; three strangers from the North gave him lime from their small betel-lime case (ufúraha wa tokā) which miraculously sufficed to build the first stone mosque; his vaulted masonry tomb receives sádaka offerings in times of calamity • The 3 Petrified Sabbath-Breakers of Mombasa (jía, p. 119): Three fishermen turned to stone (Makame iwe, Kiwemtu, Mku gnombe) for catching fish on siku ya kibunsi (Saturday Sabbath) • Parable of the Angel, Scholar (manajuóni), Toddy-Tapper (mgéma) & Rich Lady (massa, pp. 206–207) & Legend of Submerged Ungama (Formosa Bay near Malindi, swallowed by the sea for washing with milk and wasting bread, p. 405)

entries.english: Swahili Psychology of the Soul & Dreams (Rokho vs. Kifuli ja Rokho / Koma), the Ku Punga Pepo Exorcism Ritual & Widow's Purification (Krapf 1882)
entries.translation: Soul, Shade & Dreaming (ndóto p. 276, roho p. 316): Distinguishes rokho (the physical breath and chest pulsation at misho wa kifúa, which dies and decays with the body) from kifuli ja rokho (the immortal shade of the spirit, which becomes the ancestral koma after death). In dreams, 'Mimi nimelála kigógo laken kifúli ja rokhoyangu kimballi' ('I slept like a log, but the shade of my spirit was far off'), where the living kifuli meets the kifuli of the dead to exchange news ('viaonána viapána khábari'); hence taboos against treading on peeled sugarcane bark at night or upsetting a kettle • Ku Punga Pepo Spirit-Appeasement Ceremony (púnga pp. 311–312, pagáro p. 293, singa p. 340, yungi p. 431): After divination with the mbúruga board (ubáo wa ku tezamia), the mganga boils medicinal roots for 3 days (yuwapika niúngu siku tatu), then fans the patient morning and evening for 7 days with a perfumed mguisho fly-whisk (made of singa za niúmbu tail-hair) while attendants clap and beat brass plates (ubatu wa sifúri) and sorghum-stalk rattles (makayamba); after 3 days of drumming (ngóma ya púngoa), the spirit greets 'Salam aleikum' thrice, declares 'Mimi ni jinni wa jinani wa kitíti ja bahari' ('I am the Jin of the deep under the sand of the sea'), demands a turban (kilemba), livestock, and a feast-table (janu) with wali, ambari, udi, miski, tibu, ilki, and yungi (water-lily), tastes the ear-lobe blood and dishes, shakes hands with bystanders, and departs saying 'Kua heri fundi, kua heri káimu' • Widow's Mourning & Sea Purification (ku ondóa usúka, p. 412): After 3 months of seclusion (ku keti ēda) sitting on the ground and walking only on wooden clogs (mitawanda), the widow is immersed 7 times in the sea (ku sama na ku suka) while her household vessels are washed

entries.english: 5 Handful Measures (Óya), Dry Weights (Farasila/Pishi/Kebába), 5 Ingredients of Uráibu Betel-Chew, 13 Women's Ornaments (Urémbo) & Natural History Catalogues (Krapf 1882)
entries.translation: 5 Graduated Handful & Fist Terms (óya, p. 291): (1) óya (pl. nióya: single open handful; 4 nióya = 2 makoffi = 1 kebába), (2) koffi (pl. makoffi: double-handful with both palms joined), (3) konsi (compressed single handful), (4) mgnánda (pl. mignanda: finger-pinch/handful, e.g., mgnanda wa támbi vermicelli), (5) dópa / jópa / topa (handful bundle of ropes, sticks, or fito), plus ngúmi (clenched fist for striking) • Dry Measures & Weights (pishi p. 305, rotteli p. 316, wakía p. 422): 1 farasila = 12 manni = 35 rotteli (lbs); 12 pishi = 72 rotteli; 1 pishi = 4 kebába = 6 rotteli; 1 kebába = 2 makoffi = 4 nióya (~1.5 lbs); 1 wakía = weight of 1 silver reali dollar (112–140铜 pesa/pice per dollar, p. 302) • 5 Ingredients of Uráibu Betel-Chew (uráibu p. 409, tămbú p. 357, tōkā p. 375): (1) pŏpó (areca nut), (2) kattu (reddish Arabian gum), (3) tōkā (shell/coral lime kept in ufúraha case), (4) tămbū (aromatic betel leaf), (5) tómbăko (tobacco, best from Usambara & Kikuyu, p. 376); chewed red refuse is utémbe (p. 414) • 13 Swahili Women's Ornaments (urémbo, pp. 409–410) & 7 Bead Varieties (ushánga, p. 410): (1) mkuffu (neck chain), (2) kekée za mikóno (solid bracelets), (3) mitáli ya mágú (anklets), (4) halihali la fetha (silver anklet), (5) kuugési ya mkono (armlet), (6) mezi wa fetha (silver crescent), (7) majassi ya fetha (silver ear-lobe discs in ndéwe, p. 274), (8) kijáluba cha fetha kifuani (silver breast-box), (9) mashámili ya shikío (ear drops), (10) péte ya shikío (ear-ring), (11) kikuku cha sifuri/pembe (brass/ivory ring), (12) kipini cha rusasi shikíoni (ear/nose stud), (13) useja cha ushanga (bead collar), plus utondóti silver pectoral pendant (p. 415); 7 Bead Types: matúrji (white), kigeti/kiketi (blue), samesame/useja (red coral), msamli, wa sini (white porcelain), wa marjáni (coral), wa kimbosange • Rice States & Varieties (ndúme pp. 276–277, tenga p. 367): mpúnga (unhusked paddy) → ndúme za mpúnga (half-husked grains) → mtelle/mchelle (cleaned rice; coarse flour tenga vs. fine flour teléle, p. 365) → wali (boiled rice: dry separate grains pukute ya wali, watery mashendéa, bottom scorched crust ukóko, top ember-dried crust utándu, overnight rice wali wa muikū); 8 rice cultivars: bungala, garofu, kapuai, kifungo, madévu, muanga, sifara, uchukui • Natural History Catalogues: 6 Bee species (niúki, pp. 283–284, incl. intoxicating niuki wa tungáma & tiny sweet uembémbe, p. 393), 53 Kimvita Bird species (niúni, p. 284: ndiwa, kipúre, kúsi, mlámla, gandegande ... kiboróro), and 63 Coastal Fish species (sámăki, pp. 322–323: kumbu, msípue, simu, pueza, gisi ... kikánde, tangu)

entries.english: A. C. Madan's (1903, pp. ix–xvii) Conspectus II of 8 Noun Declensions (D 1–D 8), Size-Shifting Across Declensions (ki- / — / ji-, ma-, ka-) & 8 Verb-Stems (Pr., Ap., Cs., Rp., Rf., Rd., Rv., St.)
entries.translation: Conspectus II of 8 Noun Declensions (pp. xvi–xvii): D 1 m-/wa- (mtu, living beings; adj. m, mw / wa, w; pron. huyu, yule / hawa, wao; verb ni, u, a / tu, m, wa) • D 2 m-/mi- (mti, plants; adj. m, mw / mi, m; pron. huu, ule / hii, ile; verb u, w / i, y) • D 3 ki-/vi- (kitu, diminutives; adj. ki, ch / vi, vy; pron. hiki, kile / hivi, vile; verb ki, ch / vi) • D 4 u-, w-/ny- (uimbo, abstracts mostly; adj. m, mw / n; pron. huu, ule / hizi, zile; verb u, w / zi) • D 5 —/ma- (kasha, amplificatives & foreign words; adj. — / ma, m; pron. hili, lile / haya, yale; verb li, l / ya) • D 6 —/— (kazi, foreign words; adj. n; pron. hii, ile / hizi, zile; verb i, y / zi) • D 7 —/— (mahali, local only — the sole noun in D 7; adj. pa, p; pron. hapa, pale; verb pa) • D 8 —/— (kufa, verbal; adj. ku, kw; pron. huku, kule; verb ku, kw) • Size-Shifting & Diminutives (pp. 115–116, 123, 138, 200): kipete (D 3, small ring) → pete (D 6, ordinary ring) → pete/mapete (D 5, large ring); chombo → jombo (ampl. ji-ombo) → kijombo (dim. ki-ji-ombo); nyumba → jumba → chumba / kijumba; emphatic diminutive ka- (katoto tiny child, kajiwe tiny stone, kagongo kafupi very short little club, kadogo infinitesimally small) • 8 Verb-Stems (pp. xi–xiii): (1) Primary (Pr.), (2) Applied (Ap. -i-/-e-, doubled -ili-/-ele-), (3) Causal (Cs. -z-/-sh-/-s-/-y- in 6 varieties: simple, compulsive, permissive, suasive, passive, consequential), (4) Reciprocal (Rp. -an- in 5 aspects: reciprocal, connected, combined, interaction -mana, potential -kana), (5) Reflexive (Rf. ji-), (6) Reduplicated (Rd.), (7) Reversive (Rv. -u-/-o-), (8) Stative (St. -am-/-aman-)

entries.english: 7 Native Sailing Vessels (Chombo), Shipwright Hull & Rigging (Mlingoti / Foromali / Henza) & 6 Varieties of Firearms (Bunduki) in Madan (1903)
entries.translation: 7 Native Sailing Vessels (chombo p. 44, ghangi p. 82): (1) mtepe (sewn-plank Lamu/Bajuni vessel), (2) betela, (3) batili, (4) bágala (high-sterned Indian dhow), (5) bedeni, (6) awesia, (7) ghangi / ghanja (lower-sterned than bágala); vs. smaller craft: dau (sharp at both ends), mtumbwi (dugout canoe), galawa (dugout with matengo outriggers and sail, p. 79), hori (raised-stem creek canoe, p. 102), mashua (plank-built boat or steam launch, p. 211); vs. foreign ships: merikebu (ya matanga sailing, ya moshi/dohani steamer, ya kazi freight, meli passenger mail-steamer, p. 223), manowari (man-of-war, p. 207) • Hull, Mast & Rigging (pp. 44, 67–68, 71, 80, 84–85, 91, 97, 113, 128–129, 170, 237): kiunzi / maunzi (wooden hull frame, pp. 170, 213), mkuku (keel, p. 234), msitamu (false keel carrying mast), omo / gubeti (prow / projecting figurehead kikono cha omo, p. 85) vs. shetri (stern) & feuli (stern baggage cabin, p. 68), kanadili (stern projecting closet, p. 129), bumia (stern-post), fashini (wood block fastening rudder msukani to bumia, p. 67), gana / kana (tiller handle, p. 80), mlingoti (wa mbele/omoni foremast, wa kalme/galme mizzen-mast, wa maji bowsprit, p. 237; secured by mwashiri longitudinal beams and fundo cross-beam, pp. 75, 227), foromali (mainyard, p. 71), henza (thick halyard passing over masthead sheave with gofia pulley linked to deck abedari pulley by smaller jarari rope, pp. 84, 97, 113), baraji & hamarawi (fore-braces, pp. 71, 91), matilo (after-yard security rope, p. 213), goshi (windward side/tack; kalia goshi have windward advantage, p. 85) vs. demani (leeward sheet), kalafati (caulking with chembeu iron, p. 126), gadi (shoring props in gudi/majahaba dock, pp. 79, 85, 203) • 6 Varieties of Firearms (bunduki, pp. 31–32, 86): (1) bunduki ya jiwe / ya gumegume (flintlock), (2) b. ya mrao (matchlock), (3) b. ya kushindiliwa / ya fataki (muzzle-loader / percussion cap loaded with mdeki ramrod, p. 221), (4) b. ya kuvunja / ya kukunja (hinged breech-loading sporting rifle), (5) b. ya viasi (cartridge breech-loader), (6) b. ya midomo miwili / ya kasiba mbili (double-barrelled gun), plus trade guns b. ya kindoro and b. ya makoa

entries.english: 19 Customary Fees, Gratuities & Perquisites (Ada / Bakshishi), 5 Shades of Bassi in Bargaining & 8 Epistolary Epithets (Dibaji) in Madan (1903)

(2) 'Cannot you say a little more?' (3) 'Have you made your last offer?' (4) 'Wait a bit, let me think', (5) 'Agreed! Done!' • Intonation of A / Ehee (pp. 1, 57–58): Rising intonation A-aa / A-haa / A-hee / Ehee = assent ('yes, just so'); falling intonation Aa-a / A-a-a / Ee-he = dissent ('no, by no means'); prolonged final -e-e-e raised in pitch proportionally to distance (kule-e-e, akaenda e-e-e, p. 57) • 8 Epistolary Epithets in Letter Introductions (dibaji, p. 53): jenab, muhebb, akram, nasihi, azizi, hashamu, karamu, fathili, closed with katabahu bijedihi ('he wrote it by the hand of', p. 133) and the charm consonants of Kitimiri (dog of the Seven Sleepers, p. 167)

entries.english: Anatomy & Silk Embroidery of the Zanzibari Kanzu, Kitanda Bedstead, Kitanda cha Mfumi Loom & Traditional Architecture (Mlango / Kiwambaza / Kuti, Madan 1903)
entries.translation: Anatomy & Silk Stitch-Work of the Kanzu (kanzu p. 130, jabali p. 112, kiboko p. 140, kiguu p. 146, kikwapa p. 151, kinara p. 155, kipaji pp. 159–160, lisani p. 197, mhalbori p. 227, mjusi p. 230, mkia p. 232): Graded as kanzu ya kufuta (plain white without stitching), kanzu ya ziki (white cotton neck-stitching), kanzu ya kazi (red/white silk ornamental stitching), ya bafta, or ya huthurungi (yellowish-brown Arabian calico, p. 104); structural & embroidered parts include badani (main body), kaba (neck/shoulder lining, p. 123), kikwapa (underarm gore), taharizi & sijafu, jabali (raised line of needlework across the back), lisani (flap under front opening), mhalbori (lining strip under front silk stitching), viboko vya shingo (zigzag silk collar embroidery), vinara vya shingo (pillar-motifs on collar), mjusi (lizard-shaped silk motif on chest), mkia wa mjusi (silk lines running up from the lizard motif), kipaji / kiguu (4 'little feet' projections on either side of the mjusi), tiki, mrera, and tarizi; worn under a kisibau (open waistcoat: cha mikono sleeved, cha kikwapa sleeveless, cha vitana lined, cha kufuta plain, p. 164), juba (collared jacket, p. 120), mfuria (sleeveless collared coat, p. 225), or joho (embroidered woollen cloak, p. 119) • Kitanda Bedstead & Kitanda cha Mfumi Loom (kitanda pp. 165–166, mfumo p. 225, mladi pp. 235–236): Bedstead has 2 side-pieces (mfumbati), 2 end-pieces (kitakizo), 4 legs (matendegu), head (mchago), space underneath (mvungu), and corded lacing (kiwambo cha kitanda); Weaver's Loom (kitanda cha mfumi) uses mdoshi (treadle pedal raising warp threads mtande, p. 221), faraka / mfariki (comb-like thread divider, pp. 66, 223), marufaa (small warp-stretching boards, p. 210), kashabu (wooden web-parting rod, p. 132), and mladi / upanga (wooden batten tightening the woof mshindio) • Traditional House-Building, Doors & Coconut-Leaf Thatch (mlango p. 236, kiwambaza pp. 170–171, kuti pp. 186–187, kokoto p. 174): Walls (kiwambaza) of upright poles (nguzo), cross-poles (mbati / mkingiko, pp. 216, 233), rafters (kombamoyo, p. 175), and sticks (fito) plastered with kneaded clay (kandika, p. 129); concrete roofs/floors laid over boriti mangrove poles (ikiza, p. 106) with kifusi bed (fusia, p. 78), light coral stone (matumbawe, p. 213), and graded gravel (makokoto ya ndimu lime-sized, ya malimau lemon-sized, ya nazi coconut-sized, p. 174) beaten with wooden rammers (kipande, p. 159); 3 styles of plaited coconut-leaf (kuti, pp. 186–187): (a) kuti la kumba / fumba (whole leaf plaited on both sides for fences), (b) kuti la pande (fronds plaited to one side), (c) makuti ya viungo (3-ft leaf-rib upongoo sections for roofing thatch); 2 native door types (mlango, p. 236): (1) single screen door of mwale raphia mid-ribs, (2) carved double folding door of 2 boards (ubau) with centre strip (mfaa, p. 223) turning on wooden pivots in top/bottom socket strips (kimandu, p. 153) within side-posts (mwimo) and threshold/lintel (kizingiti, p. 172), barred with komeo/kiwi/kipingwa

entries.english: Zanzibari Social Groups (Mhadimu / Bohora / Khoja), Artisan Guilds (Chama), the 1872 Hurricane Epoch (Kimbunga), Confectionery (Maandasi) & 18 Perfumes (Manukato, Madan 1903)
entries.translation: Zanzibari Communities & Sects (bohora p. 29, khoja p. 137, baniani p. 23, mhadimu p. 227, mgunya p. 226, makalalao p. 204, kinubi p. 157): Mhadimu (indigenous inhabitants of eastern/southern Zanzibar Island with their own dialect and customs), Mgunya (coast people between Mombasa and the Juba using mtepe vessels), Mhindi (Muslim Indians divided into Bohora and Khoja sects, each with their own mosques, burial grounds, and clubs) vs. Baniani (non-Muslim Hindu traders, strict vegetarians), Makalalao (nickname for Malagasy settlers in Zanzibar), and Wanubi (Sudanese settlers playing the kinubi harp); Plantation Overseer Hierarchy (kadamu, p. 124): (1) msimamizi (head overseer), (2) nokoa (second overseer), (3) kadamu / mkadamu (third foreman); Chief's Guard: arobaini (15-man armed bodyguard of a chief, or 40-day post-partum period, p. 15) • Guilds, Mess-Clubs & Historical Epoch: chama (club, guild, or trade union of artisans, p. 37), kikoa (rotating communal meal club during masika rains where members take turns providing the meal, vs. kula bia where each contributes at every meal, pp. 27, 149), and Kimbunga (the great Zanzibar hurricane of April 15, 1872, used as a historical epoch for reckoning dates: 'Kimbunga kikaangusha minazi na majumba yote', p. 153) • Confectionery & Breads (maandasi p. 201, mkate pp. 231–232, fuka p. 72): bumunda, ladu (spiced flour-treacle balls, p. 192), kitumbua (fritter, p. 168), mkate wa kumimina (batter cake), mkate wa kusonga, mkate wa sinia, mkate wa tambi, mkate wa mofa (millet-meal oven cake), mkate wa ngano (wheaten loaf), nyang'amba, kimanda / maandasi ya mayai (omelette, pp. 153, 201), halua (Muscat sweetmeat, p. 91), and fuka (festival rice-flour porridge with honey and spice, p. 72) • 18 Perfumes & Incenses Used in Zanzibar (manukato p. 208, kiguba p. 145): marashi (liquid scents, e.g., marashi mawaridi rose-water), meski / miski (musk), hal waridi (otto of roses, p. 90), sandali (sandalwood), dasili, undi (aloewood), ubani (frankincense), dalia (yellow cosmetic powder), maguba / kiguba (packets of pandanus mkadi leaves tied with rihani sweet basil and dalia, pp. 85, 145), garafuu & garafuu maiti, uvumba, liwa (fragrant Madagascar wood, p. 197), buhuri, tibu, kivumbasi (mosquito-repelling basil, p. 170), and afu

entries.english: Rev. W. E. Taylor's (1910, pp. 7–23, 159–161) Dialect Classification (Tables I–IV), Kimvita Phonetic System & Minimal-Pair Homonyms
entries.translation: Three Dialect Groups (pp. 7–10): (1) Southern: Ki-Unguja (Zanzibar), Ki-P'emba (Pemba, 'the Emerald Isle', where sh becomes fy), Ki-Mrima (Mainland opposite Zanzibar, where cerebral t sometimes becomes r); (2) Northern: Ki-Amu (Lamu), Ki-Pate (Pate), Ki-Gunya (Bajuni), Ki-ti-kuu (Mainland Bajuni: cerebral t → ch, j → y, sh → s, z → dh, w → v, m- → n-, vi- → zi-, yu- → u-, universal relative -o, suffix-perfect in full use, iye? for -je?, hiyau for hivi, niyao 'I am coming'); (3) Central: Ki-Mvita (Mombasa: retains dental *t* and n*d* where Southern has ch and nj; distinguishes 2nd pl. object nawapen*d*a vs. Southern ninakupen*d*ani; preserves Arabic interdentals *th*, *dh*, **dh**, **th**; distinguishes 3rd sg. possessive -akwe so wake = 'wives' vs. wakwe = 'his', p. 9 fn. 1) • Phonetics & Syllabary (pp. 11–23): 24 Roman letters + 3 diacritics + ‘ain (‘) and hamza (’, e.g., ’a ’a 'No!', ’a ’a ’a 'Not at all!', ’ee woman's 'Yes!'); sonant nasals m' (suppresses u) and n' (suppresses i) vs. blended nasals (mb, mv, nj, ng, nz) vs. oral aspirates (ch', p', k', t', *t*' drawn from mouth breath); cerebral d, t vs. dental *d*, *t*; vocal gymnastics Mng’wpe and women's velar 'click assentive' (p. 21 fn. 1) • Minimal-Pair Homonyms (pp. 159–161): k'aa (crab) vs. kaa (ember); k'amba (prawn) vs. kamba (coir cord); k'anga (guinea-fowl) vs. kanga (palm-spur) vs. kukanga (to fry); k'ata (head-pad) vs. kata (coconut ladle) vs. ka*t*a (page/section); kupiga k'ofi (clap hands) vs. kupiga kofi (box ears); mto (river) vs. m*t*o (pillow); mt'u (person) vs. m*t*u (mangrove swamp tree); n*d*oo (bucket) vs. n*d*oo! (come!); nt'a (wax) vs. n*t*'a (point/tip); n*t*'i (earth/country) vs. nt'i (ear-ring); t'ete (smallpox) vs. *t*'e*t*'e (sparks); tui (coconut cream) vs. *t*'ui (leopard); *t*upa (file) vs. *t*'upa (bottle); (ku)*t*upa (throw away) vs. (ku)*t*'upa (leap)

entries.english: Mrs. F. Burt's (1910, pp. 24–131) Ten-Class Kimvita Noun System (Class VI Monster Class), Passive Agent 'ni', Contractions & Idioms
entries.translation: Ten Noun Classes (pp. 26–27, 94–95, 129–131): Class I MT'U (m'-/wa-), Class II MTI (m'-/mi-), Class III N (n-/n-), Class IV KI (ki-/vi-), Class V (MA) ((ji-)/ma-), Class VI (JI) or 'Monster Class' (singular ji-/ø-, plural mi- with Class II u-/i- concord for gigantic or ungainly objects: jit'u → mijit'u 'ill-conditioned giant', jana → mijana 'big hulking lad', jombo → mijombo 'huge vessel', dude → midude 'bulky thing-um-a-bob', mijuto 'swollen rivers'), Class VII U (u-/nyu- & abstracts), Class VIII PA (pahali), Class IX KU (kufa), Class X MU (mwahali) • Passive Agent Preposition 'ni' ('by', pp. 69, 109–110, 180, 243, 250): In Kimvita, the personal agent after a passive verb is always introduced by ni (whereas na means 'with' an instrument): kuumwa ni (be bitten/pained by), kuwiwa ni (be owed by / in debt to), kujawa ni / kujazwa ni (be filled with), kuruk'wa ni akili (be stunned, p. 222), a*t*okwa ni ma*t*ozi (he weeps, p. 236), waitwa ni kipofu huyu (you are called by this blind man, p. 110) • Morphological Contractions & Idioms (pp. 39, 58, 91, 93, 236): nika- → nka- → k'a- → ha- (e.g., hakaakaa 'and I stayed on'), niki- → nki- → k'i- → hi-, niku- → nku- → k'u- → hu- (habitual hu-), ni*t*a- → n'*t*a- → *t*'a-; copular contractions mbwa = ni wa (mbwako, mbwao) and n*d*a = ni ya (n*d*angu, n*d*ako, n*d*ao); idiomatic -nsha- perfect of kwisha (nsha, unsha, ansha, tunsha, mnsha, wansha, p. 39 fn. 1); subject-object inversions zina Salehe (funguo) ('Salehe has the keys', lit. 'they have Salehe', p. 58 Note III) and Mji unangia mara*dh*i ('An epidemic has come into the town', p. 91 fn. 9); enclitic -t'o of thoroughness (Fungat'o haiumizi mkono 'bind thoroughly hurts not the arm', fanyet'o 'do thoroughly', p. 236)

entries.translation: 6 Named Narrators & Dialect Registers (pp. v–xvi): Hamisi wa Kayi / Khamis bin Abubekr (pure Kiunguja), Masazo (colloquial Zanzibar), Mohammed bin Abdallah bin Ali (court style), Kathi Mohammed bin Abd en Nuri (grandson of Sheikh Muhyiddin of Mombasa — Kimvita dialect), Munyi Khatibu of Mtang'ata (Mrima dialect), and Sheikh Mohammed bin Ali & Hassan bin Yusuf (Kingozi/Kiamu poetry); Zanzibar town quarter dialects (p. ix): Kokoni (Lamu & Mombasa settlers), Baghani (Harthi Arabs), Ng'ambo (freedmen) • Historical Kenyan Coast Epigrams (pp. xi–xiii): Kilindini (Mombasa) satirical couplet "Wakilindini si watu ni punda milia, / Walikuza nti yao kwa reale mia" ("The people of Kilindi are not men, they are zebras; they sold their country for a hundred dollars") and Mombasa Poet's Battle Epigram against Lamu (Waamu): "Nalishika gurumza kwa mkono kushoto, / Na mato hiyang'ariza yakawaka kana moto, / Waamu hiwafukuza kama mbuzi na ufito; / Nikatupwa majini, hapigwa chombo kizito" • Kimvita 10-Link Agentive Compound Chain in "Mwalimu Goso" (pp. 285–293 & Note 82, p. 501): kusi (south wind) → kiyambaza mzuia kusi (mud wall, stopper of south wind) → panya mzua kiyambaza (rat, borer-through of wall, from Kimvita kuzua) → paka mla panya (cat, eater of rat) → kamba mfunga paka (rope, tier of cat) → kisu mkata kamba (knife, cutter of rope) → moto mla kisu (fire, consumer of knife) → maji mzima moto (water, putter-out of fire) → ng'ombe mnwa maji (ox, drinker of water) → kupe mgandama ng'ombe (tick, sticker-to ox) → paa mla kupe (gazelle, eater of tick), executed with Kimvita 1st pl. pronoun naswi ("naswi na tuta'mua") • Highlights of the 103 Ethnographic Notes (pp. 489–503): Note 1 fungate (7-day post-wedding seclusion in the bride's house where groom's hands/feet are henna-stained); entries.translation: Pioneering Comparative Bantu Classification (Preface, pp. iii–vi, dated Dagersheim, Oct. 14, 1850): Groups the Bantu languages from the Equator to the Cape of Good Hope into a single family which he terms the "Nilo-Hamitic or Nilotic stock of languages", contrasted with the Cushitic/Nilotic Wakuafi, Masai, and Galla • Geography & Cradle of Kisuáheli (pp. iv–v): Spoken by ~350,000–400,000 souls from Barawa (1½° N) to Mozambique across the islands of Kiáma, Túla, Patta, Lámu, Káu, Mómbas, Tánga, Pémba, Sánsibar, and Kiloa; identifies Patta and Lamu and the opposite mainland as the true historical home of pure Swahili, and describes the forest-overgrown stone ruins of Malinde (weakened by Patta after the expulsion of the Portuguese and destroyed by the Galla), while contrasting island Swahili with the watu wa mrima ("people of the mountain/higher coastal land") • Six-Column Comparative Lexicon (pp. 1–64): Aligns ~1,600 English headwords across Kisuáheli (Mombasa), Kiníka (Rabai), Kikámba, Kipokómo (learned in 1845 at Takaongo from Hadji Omar, brother of Chief Bonnaia Dadia of Kalindi), Kihiáu (Yao, learned in 1848 at Mombasa from a Kamanga youth sold at Kiloa Kibendje), and Kigálla (Dana River Oromo)
